headline: Germany to Buy Half of Tank Maker KNDS for About €6.5 Billion
author: Michael Nienaber and Eyk Henning

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 6, 2026 at 2:05 AM PST 3 min read

(Bloomberg) -- Germany will acquire half of KNDS NV for about €6.5 billion ($7.3 billion), pushing plans for an initial public offering by the Franco-German tankmaker into the distant future, according to people familiar with the matter.

The German families who own 50% of the company agreed to sell their stake in the defense manufacturer to the German government, putting it on par with the French state, which owns the other half, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the decision is not yet public.
Both sides aim to sign the deal this month and finalize it in December, according to a government document seen by Bloomberg.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has committed to ramping up weapons spending in the face of Russian aggression after abandoning debt restrictions to allow an unprecedented ramp-up of the country's defense capabilities. Outlays for defense are set to rise to more than €200 billion by the end of the decade.

"To protect key defense technologies in armored vehicle manufacturing, the federal government therefore has an interest in purchasing the family's shares to prevent third parties from gaining a dominant influence over KNDS Deutschland and the potential loss of key technologies that could result," a German economy ministry spokeswoman said on Thursday. KNDS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

KNDS was created more than a decade ago through a merger of its German operations, known as Krauss-Maffei Wegmann, and French tank manufacturer Nexter. Together with German defense giant Rheinmetall AG, KNDS is building armored vehicles for the German army and its European allies, including the Leopard 2 tank, and the Puma and Boxer armored vehicles.

The deal marks a strategic shift for the family that owns half of KNDS, which had planned to sell only a 40% stake to the German state and float the remaining 10% in an IPO. But preparations for the offering were canceled twice this year given difficult market conditions in the defense sector.

The current valuation, confirmed by two people who declined to be identified discussing confidential negotiations, is lower than an offer from June, when Germany had agreed to pay about €7.2 billion for a 40% stake.
